Alaska's conservation closure removed a commercial snow-crab season from an established fleet and processors, a direct material burden distinct from the stock collapse itself.
The existing snow-crab fleet, crews, quota interests and processors lost the legal harvest and processing season; the agency expressly acknowledged substantial industry and community impacts.

Stock collapse caused much of the underlying scarcity; the government's closure removed otherwise lawful harvest opportunity. Fishery-disaster relief and subsequent seasons require separate accounting.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
Pass 3 ADF&G and NOAA closure notices document action and express industry impact.
Match vessel permits, historical landings and crew or plant work to the 2022–23 closure and disaster payments.
2023 central and southern California Dungeness crab closure
California Department of Fish and Wildlife
CDFW ended commercial Dungeness crab take in zones 3–6 after noon on April 15, 2023, to lower humpback-whale entanglement risk.
California closed an established crab fishery in defined zones for the later 2023 season to protect whales, cutting lawful work for covered vessels and crews.
Established crab vessels, crews, buyers and processors lost the later part of that season in the covered zones.

Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
Pass 3 CDFW notice supplies exact date, zones and conservation rationale.
Use zone permits, vessel landings, crew dates and processor purchases for the closed interval.
Atlantic right-whale lobster and Jonah crab gear rule
Atlantic Large Whale Take Reduction Plan amendment
NOAA imposed new gear requirements and seasonally restricted areas on established lobster and Jonah crab trap fisheries to reduce right-whale entanglement.

Congress barred manufacture and interstate distribution of rinse-off cosmetics and covered over-the-counter products containing plastic microbeads on staggered dates to protect waterways.

Shelter/rescue placements, other pet products, direct breeder sales and a later amendment may offset or alter each business's material loss; do not assume every pet store was affected.

The chaptered 2017 statute and Governor's later summary establish the 2019 breeder-source restriction and 2020 tightening; impact by store remains to verify.
Match pre-2019 retail sales and supplier contracts to post-law activity and identify shops with a materially lost animal-sales line.
2020 Maryland retail dog and cat sale ban
No More Puppy- and Kitten-Mills Act of 2018, chapter 237
Maryland prohibited retail pet stores from selling or otherwise transferring dogs and cats to address puppy- and kitten-mill harms, after a delayed implementation period.
Maryland ended an established pet-store trade to protect animals, materially reducing the covered sales of existing shops and their supplier channel.

Existing pet shops selling cats and dogs lost their covered sales and supplying breeders lost a retail customer. The legislature's fiscal and policy note expressly anticipates lower taxable sales and a lost customer for small breeders.
Direct sales from breeders and shelter displays may continue; some stores did not sell covered animals and pet supplies remain. Actual firm and worker losses require transaction records.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
Enacted law gives the restriction and delayed date; legislative fiscal note describes lost retail sales and breeder channels without proving a specific store closure.
Identify pre-ban retail pet licenses and sales, breeder contracts and post-ban animal sales or adoption arrangements.
Puppy Mill Pipeline Act, chapter 681 of 2022
New York barred pet stores from selling dogs, cats and rabbits statewide to stop the puppy-mill supply chain.
New York's animal-welfare law cut off a lawful animal-sales line for an existing, identifiable group of retail pet dealers.

Existing licensed pet dealers with retail stores lost the legal sale of those animals; the Attorney General sent a pre-effective-date notice to affected dealers and later described enforcement against a named pre-existing shop.
Animal adoptions and other pet products may continue; post-effective illegal sales are not compensable lawful work. Do not infer every licensed dealer or employee lost a primary income source.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
Official notice and Attorney General release identify effective date, covered animal sales and established licensed dealers.
Use pre-December 2024 license and sales records, later store status and lawful alternative revenue to measure the exposed group.
2019 New York City expanded-polystyrene foam ban
Local Law 142 of 2013 and DSNY implementation
New York City prohibited sale, use or possession of specified single-use expanded-polystyrene food containers and loose-fill packaging for waste-reduction purposes.
New York City stopped an established foam-product market for environmental reasons, materially affecting specialized suppliers and some small users' costs.

The city's own notice identifies foam manufacturers, distributors, stores and food-service establishments as affected. Covered product makers and distributors lost that city market; small businesses faced replacement costs and could seek hardship waivers.

Prepackaged-food and raw-meat exceptions, warning period, substitutes and waivers narrow the affected group; later state foam law is a different action and overlapping losses must not be double-counted.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
DSNY names the 2019 prohibition and exceptions; Small Business Services describes waivers for excessive financial hardship.
Find city foam suppliers and their pre-ban sales and workplaces, waiver decisions, substitute-product revenue and post-2022 statewide overlap.
Garrison Dam flooding of Fort Berthold land
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
The United States built Garrison Dam for regional flood control, power and other public purposes, filling Lake Sakakawea on the Missouri River.
A federal dam built for broad flood-control and power benefits flooded established Fort Berthold homes and working land, materially burdening a concentrated community.
GAO records 152,360 acres flooded on the Fort Berthold Reservation; Interior had estimated 289 families in the flood area. Homes, ranches and all of the reservation's irrigable land were affected.

Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
GAO Table 1 quantifies reservation flood acreage and family exposure; the Corps confirms project and public purposes.
Reconcile the original land acquisition and tribal compensation records with affected farms, enterprises and later settlements.
Oahe Dam flooding of Cheyenne River and Standing Rock lands
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
The United States constructed Oahe Dam as part of the Missouri River system to reduce downstream flood risk and provide power, water and navigation benefits.
A federal public-benefit reservoir permanently flooded Cheyenne River and Standing Rock land, materially affecting established homes and land-based work.
GAO records 104,420 acres flooded on the Cheyenne River Reservation and 55,994 on Standing Rock, including valuable river bottoms, resources, structures and land-based livelihoods.

Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
GAO Table 1 ties both reservation areas to Oahe; the Corps describes system public purposes.
Compare dam-specific land files, ranch and farm uses, relocation and compensation on the two reservations.
Fort Randall Dam flooding of reservation lands
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
The United States built Fort Randall Dam for Missouri River flood control and related public power and water purposes.
Federal reservoir construction for regional benefits displaced families and working land on several reservations, with losses attributable to this dam to be separately measured.
GAO ties this dam to lost land at Crow Creek, Lower Brule and Yankton; it reports 119 families displaced at Crow Creek and Lower Brule by Fort Randall, with 2,851 acres flooded at Yankton.

Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel. Crow Creek and Lower Brule total acreage in GAO combines this dam with Big Bend; do not assign all acreage twice.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
GAO ties these reservations and 119 displaced families to Fort Randall; combined acreage cannot be split from its summary.
Use dam-specific condemnation and relocation records to allocate losses separate from Big Bend and credit original and later compensation.
Big Bend Dam flooding of Crow Creek and Lower Brule lands
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
The United States constructed Big Bend Dam as another Missouri River flood-control and hydropower project.
Big Bend's federal public-benefit reservoir separately displaced an established Crow Creek and Lower Brule group, despite overlapping earlier flood effects.
GAO reports 89 families displaced on Crow Creek and Lower Brule by Big Bend; the two reservations also lost land to Fort Randall.

Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel. Some families faced both projects, so the same loss cannot be counted twice.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
GAO states the 89-family Big Bend displacement and overlapping Fort Randall effects, and lists original settlement acts.
Match parcel and household relocation across both dam projects, distinguishing incremental Big Bend harm and prior compensation.
Gavins Point Dam flooding of Santee land
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
The United States built Gavins Point Dam within the Missouri River flood-control and power system.
Federal dam construction for the wider Missouri basin permanently took a smaller group's established reservation land and resources.
GAO identifies 593 acres of Santee Reservation land permanently flooded by this dam, with land and natural-resource impacts.

Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
GAO Table 1 assigns the 593 acres to Gavins Point and describes general reservation damages and compensation.
Identify affected Santee parcels and uses, initial property payments and any subsequent compensation.
Grand Coulee Dam and Lake Roosevelt inundation
United States / Bureau of Reclamation and federal works agencies
The federal government built Grand Coulee Dam and filled Lake Roosevelt to generate power, irrigate the Columbia Basin and support public works.
A federal dam for national power and irrigation inundated established towns, homes and fishing places, materially affecting smaller resident and working groups.
The National Park Service reports that 11 river towns were lost and roughly 3,000 people left homes in the inundation zone; Kettle Falls and its longstanding salmon fishing place were also covered.
Residents, tribal fishing communities and town businesses had different land rights and redress histories. Do not treat everyone who moved as having the same unpaid livelihood loss.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NPS identifies the 11 lost towns, roughly 3,000 displaced people and the river-bottom communities; project purposes and compensation need individualized group review.
Match flooded parcels, town enterprises and tribal fishing use to the original acquisition and later settlement records.
Norris Dam reservoir relocation in the Clinch Valley
TVA built Norris Dam for flood control and power as its first planned hydroelectric project, acquiring and flooding upstream land.
TVA's public power and flood project displaced established Clinch Valley households and land-based work through the dam land program.
A National Park Service history says the project established a relocation protocol for families and grave sites; the Clinch Valley record describes community displacement.
The public source establishes an affected resident group but not a final family count or loss after land payments; some acquired owners could continue farms elsewhere.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NPS nomination documents relocation protocol; TVA identifies dam timing and power/flood purposes. Scale requires original land records.
Extract TVA purchase and relocation ledgers to identify farms, businesses and actual resettlement results.
Watauga Dam relocation of Butler, Tennessee
TVA built Watauga Dam to control flooding and generate power and moved Butler, Tennessee, to higher ground before reservoir filling.
A federal flood-control and power project moved a preexisting agricultural town, materially affecting its households and place-bound livelihoods.
TVA describes Butler as an agricultural town of about 650 families when work resumed; moving the whole town disrupted existing homes, farms and local businesses.
The 650 is a pre-project town-family figure, not a count of uncompensated moves or lost businesses; Butler was rebuilt and some activities resumed.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
TVA records the town's relocation and family context plus dam completion and public purpose; net loss requires local records.
Use TVA relocation and property ledgers to distinguish land loss, resettlement, replacement enterprises and prior payment.
1942 wartime exclusion and incarceration of Japanese Americans
Executive Order 9066 and civilian exclusion orders
The federal government asserted a nationwide wartime-defense purpose, designated military areas and forcibly removed and incarcerated Japanese Americans from the West Coast.

Federal exclusion orders asserted national defense while imposing devastating material loss on a smaller American group; later Congress rejected the premise and provided redress, which must be counted.
More than 120,000 people were uprooted; many lost homes, property, businesses and work. The displaced cohort included U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents.

Congress later recognized the action as a grave injustice rooted in racial prejudice and war hysteria, not a valid military necessity. The 1948 property-claims law and 1988 redress payments must be credited; this record does not suggest any additional individual entitlement.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured

NPS documents the order and 120,000-plus forced removals; National Archives explains the later congressional apology and $20,000 redress. Stated national-security purpose is expressly described as a claim later repudiated.
Match business and work loss categories to contemporaneous records and the two redress programs, without relitigating the event's wrongful character.
1857 Seneca Village clearance for Central Park
State-authorized eminent domain for Central Park
New York City used eminent domain to acquire Seneca Village land and remove residents to build a large public park for the growing city.
The city took and cleared an established smaller community for a public park, materially ending its homes, place-based cultivation and local institutions.

City and NPS histories describe at least 220 established residents, homes, churches, a school, fields and orchards displaced from this community, including Black property owners and immigrant neighbors.
Original property payments, tenant status and subsequent work or housing need separate evidence; do not infer that all residents owned land or received no compensation.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NYC Landmarks documents community displacement and resident count; NYC Parks supplies the public-park authorization and eminent-domain purpose.
Cross-check property award and census records against residents' homes, crops, businesses and tenancy.
District of Columbia / federal redevelopment agencies
D.C. Redevelopment Act and Southwest renewal plans
Federal and District planners assembled and cleared Southwest Washington land for a public urban-renewal program intended to improve housing and the capital's economy.
Public urban renewal cleared established Southwest homes and enterprises for wider city development, concentrating material loss in the affected neighborhood.
The National Capital Planning Commission reports 400 acres cleared, forced removal of 23,500 residents and displacement of local small businesses; many could not return.
The large group includes households and firms with different losses, acquisition payments and relocation assistance. Later redevelopment jobs do not automatically erase particular earlier harms.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NCPC official history gives 400 acres and 23,500 people; NCPC separately identifies condemned small businesses and the urban-improvement purpose.
Match renewal parcels, businesses and displaced households to acquisition and relocation files and subsequent compensation.
1950s I-375 Detroit highway and urban renewal clearance
Michigan and United States / highway agencies
I-375 construction and related urban renewal
Michigan and federal highway agencies built I-375 to create an urban transportation link, with associated redevelopment in central Detroit.
The public highway project removed an established residential and commercial district, materially affecting its local businesses and residents.
Federal Highway Administration records say the route and subsequent urban renewal largely demolished Paradise Valley and Black Bottom, established Black residential and business centers.
The highway and following renewal are overlapping but distinguishable government actions; property payments, exact parcels and businesses need allocation before counting losses twice.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
FHWA documents construction in two established neighborhoods and demolition; its workshop distinguishes subsequent urban renewal.
Compare historic right-of-way, condemnation and business directories to identify highway-specific and renewal-specific burdens.
New London Fort Trumbull economic-development takings
New London authorized land assembly and condemnation in the Fort Trumbull district to pursue citywide economic revitalization and jobs.
A city used eminent domain on a smaller property group for a stated wider economic-development benefit, imposing a material land and place-based burden.

The plan contained about 115 parcels with residential and commercial uses; after voluntary purchases, the city initiated condemnation against owners who refused to sell, uprooting the remaining place-bound homeowners and businesses.

Most parcels were purchased voluntarily; the Supreme Court case concerns the remaining condemned group. Fair-market land awards and relocation assistance must be credited, and unrealized redevelopment benefits do not measure a particular owner's loss.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
Connecticut legislative research describes the 90-acre/115-parcel plan; Supreme Court opinion identifies compulsory proceedings after voluntary acquisitions and the stated public economic purpose.
Use city condemnation dockets and relocation files to isolate compelled properties, affected enterprises and paid amounts.
1942 Oak Ridge Manhattan Project land acquisition
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
Manhattan Project Oak Ridge site acquisition
The Army acquired and fenced 56,000 acres for a secret wartime uranium-enrichment center serving national defense.
A national-defense project took established rural land and work in one local area, imposing concentrated material costs.
National Park Service records identify longstanding rural communities whose homes, land and livelihoods were displaced by the site's acquisition.
Original purchase or condemnation payments, temporary wartime jobs and later land use may offset different households differently; acreage is site size, not a count of uncompensated farms.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NPS identifies displaced established communities and livelihoods; DOE documents the 1942–43 acquisition and 56,000-acre security perimeter.
Review federal land-acquisition files and community records for affected farms, shops and compensation.
1942 Los Alamos Manhattan Project land acquisition
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
Manhattan Project Los Alamos laboratory site acquisition
The Army acquired the Pajarito Plateau for the wartime weapons laboratory, removing homesteaders and closing the Los Alamos Ranch School.
A federal wartime laboratory displaced an established small homesteading and school community to serve national defense.

NPS records identify local Hispanic and other homesteaders who abandoned cabins and farm use; 12 homesteads remained with original owners and seven with their families at acquisition, while the established ranch school closed.
Some residents later worked at the laboratory. Tribal cultural and land interests are distinct from a homestead owner's loss; property and school settlements must be credited.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NPS documents homesteader and school removal and a 19-homestead original/family ownership subset, not total displaced individuals.
Match the 1942 acquisition files to homesteads, seasonal farm uses, ranch school business and later work.
United States / Army Corps of Engineers
Manhattan Project Hanford site land requisition
The United States took Columbia River land for the Hanford plutonium-production project, ordering residents out on short notice for wartime defense work.
A national-defense land requisition removed established farms, homes and businesses in one local area for a wider wartime project.
NPS reports roughly 1,500 residents in White Bluffs, Hanford, Richland and nearby communities affected, including farmers and local enterprises; some owners had 30–90 days to leave.
Initial settlements, wartime replacement work and Native land and use interests differ by group; the 1,500 is a population estimate, not a job-loss or unpaid-claim count.
Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
NPS identifies communities, approximate resident group and short notice; site-specific compensation must be reconciled.
Review requisition, farm and business records and original settlements; separate tribal use interests from private holdings.

Pacific sardine primary directed fishery established fleet

Check permits, landings, crew earnings, other fisheries and disaster payments; not an individual entitlement finding.

Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet fishery established fleet

Check permits, landings, crew earnings, other fisheries and disaster payments; not an individual entitlement finding.
Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet fishery established fleet

Check permits, landings, crew earnings, other fisheries and disaster payments; not an individual entitlement finding.
Affected product makers and ingredient suppliers

Affected wash makers, ingredient suppliers and private-label firms had to reformulate, relabel, obtain approvals or withdraw products. FDA modeled 2,093 affected product codes, one-time relabeling costs of $18.9–$53.4 million and potentially substantial reformulation costs.
Economic group estimate; not individual separation
Match specific companies and product lines, reformulation expense, discontinued sales and offsetting substitutions.
Affected product makers and ingredient suppliers

Existing makers of the covered products had to reformulate, relabel or discontinue them. FDA modeled about $1.07–$2.50 million in aggregate one-time reformulation and labeling costs for the affected product cohort.
Economic group estimate; not individual separation
Match specific companies and product lines, reformulation expense, discontinued sales and offsetting substitutions.
Remaining BVO beverage and flavor-concentrate users
Affected product makers and ingredient suppliers

A small cohort of beverage and flavor-concentrate makers still used BVO. FDA's analysis found eight parent companies with confirmed use in 2021 and modeled $6.6–$16.4 million in first-year industry reformulation and relabeling costs, much of which could be passed on.
Economic group estimate; not individual separation
Match specific companies and product lines, reformulation expense, discontinued sales and offsetting substitutions.

Maryland dog and cat retail stores and breeders

Existing pet shops selling cats and dogs lost their covered sales and supplying breeders lost a retail customer. The legislature's fiscal and policy note expressly anticipates lower taxable sales and a lost customer for small breeders.
Identify actual pre-ban licenses, sales, workers, alternative lines and exception use; not an individual award finding.
New York licensed retail pet dealers

Identify actual pre-ban licenses, sales, workers, alternative lines and exception use; not an individual award finding.
NYC foam foodware suppliers and affected small users

The city's own notice identifies foam manufacturers, distributors, stores and food-service establishments as affected. Covered product makers and distributors lost that city market; small businesses faced replacement costs and could seek hardship waivers.
Identify actual pre-ban licenses, sales, workers, alternative lines and exception use; not an individual award finding.

values: An effective government action for broad public benefit imposes a material cost on a smaller existing group; loss of a main job counts even if other work continues.
An unlisted event or group may qualify by the rule. No category, geography, historical period or absence from this spreadsheet bars a petition.
This is an event-level research ledger, not a roll of people eligible for relief.
Source checks document actions and publicly identified burden; worksite and group details may require later certification work.

The continuous register has 231 qualifying event-level entries after six supplemental sweeps. Every retained row has a plain-language rule explanation and at least one linked source, but the independent holdout found additional obvious historical examples. It is a substantial open starting point, not an estimated majority or a closed category list. The principal remaining research is a bounded inventory of smaller BRAC actions, seasonal fishery orders, state/local bans, public project takings and site-level affected groups, with separate accounting for competing causes and past compensation.
The same material-effect standard governs every event. The register is nonexclusive; a lost main job can be material even if other work continues.

Attempted to reopen all 92 primary anchors, replaced or sharpened 13 weak links or timing descriptions, and corrected the TCE timing caveat. Direct fetching of several older or PDF anchors remains imperfect; the ledger flags that limit rather than treating retrieval as worker-level proof.

Mechanism sweep added 11 event records in the same continuous register: park land acquisition, defense base closure, irrigation curtailment, ozone and solvent controls, tobacco quota repeal, public-health business shutdown, and fishery/gear restrictions. The search did not enumerate all local actions or every annual fishery order.

Independent holdout search found five more qualifying records (microbeads, new small engines, farm-confinement sales standards, and two earlier BRAC bases). GAO lists scores of earlier major BRAC closures and says aggregate eminent-domain data are lacking. This document is a substantial starting register; a claim of a majority or vast majority cannot yet be measured.

Official GAO Appendix IV inventory yielded 71 additional named major 1988–1995 BRAC sites beyond Kelly and McClellan already listed. The 73 sites total 129,649 estimated civilian jobs lost and 79,740 redevelopment jobs created by October 2001. These are distinct worksite events, not person-specific claims or a complete BRAC universe.

Cross-checked GAO's list of 23 actually closed major 2005 BRAC installations against Commission position projections; 17 additional closures with identified civilian or contractor groups are retained. Five distinct Alaska crab and California Dungeness seasons were added from agency records. Preliminary BRAC job figures and natural stock losses are not presented as actual individual layoffs.

Cross-checked 71 previously entered major 1988–1995 BRAC sites to a later GAO table that identifies each exact decision round. Added Kansas City MCSA and the separate 2004 Roosevelt Roads closure with workforce limits. Galena's major employment decline preceded its 2005 closure; the chemical-depot sites require mission-completion causation review.

Added the 2015 directed Pacific sardine closure and four distinct 2021–24 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet seasons using NOAA/ADF&G action and impact records. Seasonal restrictions, natural stock declines, alternate fisheries and disaster aid are differentiated.

Federal FDA inventory added three enacted product restrictions with official economic analyses: consumer antibacterial washes, antiseptic rubs, and BVO in food. Powdered-glove and proposed chemical rules were held because existing records did not establish the required material effect or a final effective ban.

Added California, Maryland and New York pet-store restrictions and NYC's 2019 foam ban from enacted law and implementation records. Oregon and Washington pet-store leads were not added because their grandfathering preserves qualifying preexisting sellers; each retained event requires group-specific material-effect evidence.

Added eight public-project events: five separate Missouri River dams documented in GAO's reservation and compensation table, Grand Coulee's inundated towns, and TVA Norris and Watauga relocations. Overlapping Fort Randall/Big Bend harms and prior land or tribal compensation are explicit controls.

Independent historical holdout added eight distinct events: wartime Japanese American exclusion, Seneca Village, Southwest Washington urban renewal, Detroit I-375, Fort Trumbull, and Manhattan Project land acquisition at Oak Ridge, Los Alamos and Hanford. Exact ID/why/source counts reconcile; overlapping project harms and earlier compensation remain explicit. The holdout found omissions, so no majority-coverage percentage is claimed.

censusIntroduction.text: These are government actions that pursued a benefit for the public as a whole while placing a material cost on a smaller, existing trade or group. For a state or local action, the relevant public is that jurisdiction's community. The burden can be lost work, an ended product or harvest market, a forced change in established operations, or another material livelihood effect; it need not be a proven layoff or the complete end of a person's career. This is a substantial starting point, not a claim to have found every such event.

Every item below clears that event-level screen. The plain-language explanation comes first, followed by its screening disposition and the more detailed record. Later work can measure a particular worksite or occupation group's losses, assess competing causes and prepare certification files. Inclusion here does not establish that every worker or firm in an industry was harmed, and this document does not advocate for particular people.

The list is open. An unlisted action or affected group may qualify under the same rule, regardless of industry, jurisdiction, period, or resemblance to these examples. A person can lose a principal job and suffer a material loss while still holding another job. A petition must be decided by the rule and its evidence, never by whether the event already appears in this register.

Stable IDs preserve links to the evidence spreadsheet; missing numbers reflect research leads that did not clear this screen. The salmon seasons are separate government actions. The citation audit distinguishes reopened anchors, corrected links and sources whose direct text still requires verification; a source check does not prove a particular worksite loss.

The event screen and Cornerstone eligibility rule remain unchanged. Section 4 of the Fourteenth Amendment separately prohibits the United States and every state from paying any claim for the loss or emancipation of an enslaved person, and declares such claims illegal and void. That constitutional limit resolves a claim for compensation arising from emancipation regardless of the former owner's loyalty or state of residence; no additional Cornerstone exclusion is needed.

An official GAO inventory of 73 named major 1988–1995 BRAC sites with estimated civilian job losses is represented with exact decision rounds. The register names 18 of 23 major installations actually closed in the 2005 round where a baseline workforce projection or other group record supports a material effect; the other five need further causation review. Some smaller and separately authorized closures are also included, but their universe is not enumerated. GAO found no aggregate count adequate to measure the business and household effects of eminent-domain redevelopment. Many other jurisdiction and period inventories remain open.

The continuous register has 231 qualifying event-level entries after six supplemental sweeps. Every retained row has a plain-language rule explanation and at least one linked source, but the independent holdout found additional obvious historical examples. It is a substantial open starting point, not an estimated majority or a closed category list. The principal remaining research is a bounded inventory of smaller BRAC actions, seasonal fishery orders, state/local bans, public project takings and site-level affected groups, with separate accounting for competing causes and past compensation.
Coverage sources.  GAO major BRAC sites and job estimates; GAO on eminent-domain data limits.

census.title: Shenandoah National Park land acquisition and displacement

paragraphs.text: C-122  Shenandoah National Park land acquisition and displacement

Why this qualifies.  Virginia acquired and condemned occupied mountain land for a national park, displacing smaller farming and business communities so the broader public could enjoy conservation and recreation.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Virginia and United States | 1928–1930s. Virginia bought or condemned Blue Ridge tracts to create a national park and conveyed them to the United States. Existing residents, tenant farmers, shops and mills were displaced from the park area.
Worksite and group record.  NPS identifies families, tenants, stores and mills in the affected mountain communities; individual farm and business loss requires tract records.

Causation and legal limits.  The public park purpose is clear. Payment for title and relocation varied, and eminent-domain compensation must be credited; mere residence without a material livelihood loss is not presumed.
Further event evidence.  Link parcel, tenancy and occupation records to actual acquisition dates and identify any unreimbursed material livelihood loss.

census.title: 1978 CFC aerosol-propellant ban

paragraphs.text: C-123  1978 CFC aerosol-propellant ban
Why this qualifies.  Federal ozone-protection rules ended an established CFC aerosol product line, imposing an immediate market loss and process change on its makers and workers.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  EPA and FDA | 1978–1979. Federal rules ended manufacture of bulk fluorocarbons for most aerosol propellants in October 1978, aerosol product manufacture in December, and interstate shipment of remaining stocks in April 1979 to protect the ozone layer.
Worksite and group record.  Existing fluorocarbon propellant makers, aerosol fillers and workers tied to the restricted line faced the loss of that lawful product market.
Causation and legal limits.  Exceptions and substitution to alternative propellants limit firm-specific loss; assess actual affected sales and jobs rather than assume all aerosol operations ended.
Further event evidence.  Identify covered products, historic production and affected worksite operations at each phase-in date.

census.title: 2021–22 Bristol Bay red king crab season closure

paragraphs.text: C-226  2021–22 Bristol Bay red king crab season closure
Why this qualifies.  The full-season closure protected the resource while materially removing an established fleet's harvest and processing work.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.
Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | 2021–22 season. Alaska did not open the 2021–22 Bristol Bay red king crab season to conserve a depleted stock.
Worksite and group record.  The established Bristol Bay red king crab vessel, crew and processing groups lost a full authorized harvest season.

Causation and legal limits.  ADF&G's disaster request attributes the stock decline chiefly to natural conditions and estimates large combined ex-vessel losses for two seasons; season-specific government-caused loss and any relief need separate accounting.
Further event evidence.  Match 2021–22 permits, landings, crew and plant records against baseline seasons and relief payments.

Sources and citation check.  Bristol Bay red king crab opening threshold and closure (adfg.alaska.gov); Additional legal or source record (newsrelease.adfg.alaska.gov).  Official agency closure or disaster records document the action and affected fleet; seasonal and competing-cause limits are explicit.

census.title: 2022–23 Bristol Bay red king crab season closure

paragraphs.text: C-227  2022–23 Bristol Bay red king crab season closure
Why this qualifies.  The renewed conservation closure removed another full season of work from a small established fishery group.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | 2022–23 season. Alaska again kept the Bristol Bay red king crab fishery closed for the 2022–23 season because mature female abundance remained low.
Worksite and group record.  The existing red king crab fleet, crews and processors lost a second complete season of legal harvest work.

Causation and legal limits.  The stock decline, overlapping snow-crab failure and existing disaster funds are distinct; two seasons are separate decisions but the same worker must not recover twice for a common loss.
Further event evidence.  Trace this season's permit, crew, plant and ex-vessel receipts and disaster offsets separately from 2021–22.

Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.
Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | 2023–24 season. Alaska kept the Bering Sea snow crab commercial fishery closed in 2023–24 to protect the collapsed stock.

paragraphs.text: C-232  2004 congressional closure of Naval Station Roosevelt Roads

Why this qualifies.  Congress closed the naval station as part of a broad national defense and training decision, materially ending the work tied to the installation for an established civilian and contractor group.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Congress and Department of the Navy | March 31, 2004. Congress directed closure of the naval station following the end of training on Vieques, and the Navy closed it in March 2004 as a military infrastructure decision.

Worksite and group record.  The installation had an established civilian, contractor and base-dependent service workforce. Navy testimony addressed relocation and outplacement for civilian employees as it carried out the closure; contemporary reporting described substantial lost civilian employment.

census.title: 2015 closure of the primary directed Pacific sardine fishery

paragraphs.text: C-233  2015 closure of the primary directed Pacific sardine fishery
Why this qualifies.  The federal conservation rule closed a formerly productive directed sardine fishery, materially removing that source of income for its existing fleet and processors.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / NOAA Fisheries | 2015–16 fishing year. Federal managers closed the primary directed Pacific sardine fishery off Washington, Oregon and California when biomass fell below the conservation cutoff.

Worksite and group record.  Existing purse-seine vessels, crews and sardine processors lost the primary directed catch. California's official request reported a 90% lower statewide sardine ex-vessel value in 2015 than its 2010–14 average.

Causation and legal limits.  The natural biomass fall is a strong competing cause; live-bait, minor directed and incidental catch remained legal and some vessels switched species. Do not label total revenue decline as caused only by the closure.
Further event evidence.  Compare vessel-level past sardine revenue and gear permits to subsequent catch, other species, processing activity and disaster aid.

Sources and citation check.  Pacific sardine annual specification and harvest cutoff (fisheries.noaa.gov); Additional legal or source record (media.fisheries.noaa.gov).  NOAA identifies the initial 2015–16 closure; California's request reports ex-vessel impact and exceptions. Natural depletion and government restriction must be separated.

census.title: 2021 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet restrictions

paragraphs.text: C-234  2021 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet restrictions
Why this qualifies.  Alaska constrained an established setnet fleet's 2021 earning season for salmon conservation, materially affecting its operators and crews.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.
Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | 2021 season. Alaska restricted East Side setnet sockeye harvest in the 2021 season to conserve weak Kenai River Chinook salmon.

Worksite and group record.  Established East Side setnet permit holders, crew and dependent processors had fewer legal harvest opportunities; the State and NOAA later identified the 2021 fishery for disaster assistance.
Causation and legal limits.  Weak Chinook returns are an independent ecological cause; the legal fishing restrictions imposed a distinct burden, and subsequent disaster aid offsets losses.
Further event evidence.  Reconcile each 2021 inseason order and opening with permit, landing and aid records.

Sources and citation check.  Alaska salmon conservation restrictions (adfg.alaska.gov); Additional legal or source record (adfg.alaska.gov).  State request attributes reduced 2021 setnet opportunity to Chinook conservation restrictions; NOAA disaster determination confirms affected fishery, not a count of separations.

census.title: 2022 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet closure

paragraphs.text: C-235  2022 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet closure
Why this qualifies.  The July state conservation closure materially cut an existing setnet fleet's remaining fishing opportunity and associated crew work.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | July 16, 2022 and season restrictions. Alaska closed set gillnet fishing in the Kenai, Kasilof and East Forelands sections in July 2022 under Chinook conservation measures.

Worksite and group record.  Existing East Side setnet operators and crews lost legal fishing periods during their seasonal livelihood; 2022 was included in a subsequent federal fishery-disaster determination.
Causation and legal limits.  Earlier 2022 openings, natural run weakness and later disaster aid change the net effect; do not treat the whole year as closed by the July order.
Further event evidence.  Match dates and sections of all 2022 orders with permit landings, crew records and disaster disbursements.

Sources and citation check.  Emergency Order 2S-18-22 (adfg.alaska.gov); Additional legal or source record (adfg.alaska.gov).  ADF&G order names the restricted sections and date; NOAA identifies the 2022 fishery disaster. Prior openings are a limit.

census.title: 2023 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet season closure

paragraphs.text: C-236  2023 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet season closure
Why this qualifies.  The state conservation closure removed the entire scheduled East Side setnet season for an established fleet, imposing a material income and work loss.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | March 9, 2023 through season. Alaska closed East Side commercial set gillnet salmon fishing before the 2023 season to protect Kenai River king salmon; its season report states this fishery did not open that year.
Worksite and group record.  Existing setnet permit holders and crews lost that entire 2023 fishing opportunity, and the closure also reduced sockeye deliveries to dependent processors.
Causation and legal limits.  The Chinook conservation problem is a competing cause and federal disaster assistance later addressed some losses; other fisheries and jobs need separate measurement.
Further event evidence.  Use 2023 permits and past landings, crew payroll and processor purchases to measure the affected group net of aid.

Sources and citation check.  Emergency Order 2S-1-23 (adfg.alaska.gov); Additional legal or source record (adfg.alaska.gov).  ADF&G's emergency order and annual report establish a full-season failure to open; NOAA later recognized a 2023 disaster.

Why this qualifies.  Alaska's 2024 conservation order kept an established setnet fleet out of its regular season, materially removing its seasonal earning opportunity.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Alaska Department of Fish and Game | April 12–August 15, 2024. Alaska closed the East Side setnet fishery before the 2024 season for Kenai king salmon conservation; the agency's season report says it remained closed through August 15.
Worksite and group record.  Established East Side setnet operators and crews lost a second full season of this fishing activity; other Upper Cook Inlet fleets still harvested salmon.

Causation and legal limits.  Poor king salmon forecasts prompted the order, and broader Upper Cook Inlet ex-vessel results are not this fleet's actual lost earnings. Any later aid and alternative work require accounting.
Further event evidence.  Compare 2024 permit and crew records to earlier years, separate other fleets and verify later assistance.

Sources and citation check.  Emergency Order 2-F-H-2-24 (adfg.alaska.gov); Additional legal or source record (adfg.alaska.gov).  ADF&G order and season summary establish its date, full-season duration and targeted sections.

census.title: 2016 FDA consumer antibacterial-wash ingredient rule

paragraphs.text: C-238  2016 FDA consumer antibacterial-wash ingredient rule
Why this qualifies.  FDA restricted an established antibacterial-wash market for health reasons, imposing material product-line and reformulation costs on the firms that supplied it.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Food and Drug Administration | September 6, 2017 compliance. FDA determined 19 active ingredients, including triclosan and triclocarban, could no longer be marketed without drug approval in ordinary consumer antiseptic washes to protect public health.

Worksite and group record.  Affected wash makers, ingredient suppliers and private-label firms had to reformulate, relabel, obtain approvals or withdraw products. FDA modeled 2,093 affected product codes, one-time relabeling costs of $18.9–$53.4 million and potentially substantial reformulation costs.

Causation and legal limits.  Some companies anticipated the rule and voluntarily changed formulas; replacement soaps can preserve sales and work. The model is not a realized net-income or job-loss total.
Further event evidence.  Identify the affected SKUs and ingredient suppliers and compare actual conversion, discontinued lines and cost against pre-rule baselines.

census.title: 2019 FDA consumer antiseptic-rub ingredient rule

paragraphs.text: C-239  2019 FDA consumer antiseptic-rub ingredient rule
Why this qualifies.  The federal health rule removed a defined set of formerly marketed sanitizer ingredients and imposed material product changes on the firms using them.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Food and Drug Administration | April 2019 rule; one-year compliance. FDA made 28 active ingredients in nonprescription consumer antiseptic rubs ineligible for marketing through the OTC monograph, requiring drug approval or a change to the affected sanitizer and wipe products.

Worksite and group record.  Existing makers of the covered products had to reformulate, relabel or discontinue them. FDA modeled about $1.07–$2.50 million in aggregate one-time reformulation and labeling costs for the affected product cohort.

Causation and legal limits.  Ethyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol and benzalkonium chloride were deferred and were not banned by this rule. The impact model is prospective; alternatives and other product lines limit net harm.
Further event evidence.  Match actual product lists and ingredient use to the covered 28 ingredients, then verify realized costs and displaced sales.

Sources and citation check.  Consumer Antiseptic Rub Final Rule, 84 FR 14847 (fda.gov); Additional legal or source record (fda.gov).  FDA guidance identifies the final monograph decision; FDA impact analysis identifies affected products and modeled costs while excluding deferred common ingredients.

census.title: 2024 FDA brominated-vegetable-oil food-use revocation

paragraphs.text: C-240  2024 FDA brominated-vegetable-oil food-use revocation
Why this qualifies.  FDA ended a previously lawful food-ingredient use for public health, directly forcing the remaining small group of user firms to replace formulas and labels at material cost.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Food and Drug Administration | August 2, 2024 effective; transition period. FDA revoked permission to use brominated vegetable oil as a stabilizer in food after concluding the available evidence no longer supported its safety.

Worksite and group record.  A small cohort of beverage and flavor-concentrate makers still used BVO. FDA's analysis found eight parent companies with confirmed use in 2021 and modeled $6.6–$16.4 million in first-year industry reformulation and relabeling costs, much of which could be passed on.

Causation and legal limits.  Most large beverage makers had already switched voluntarily; FDA expected low incremental long-run costs and replacement formulas. Model costs cannot be assumed to be job losses or a material net loss for each firm.
Further event evidence.  Verify affected 2024–25 products, actual formula and label expenditure, cost pass-through and discontinued lines for the remaining users.

Sources and citation check.  Final rule revoking 21 CFR 180.30, 89 FR 55040 (fda.gov); Additional legal or source record (fda.gov).  FDA confirms the final revocation and timing; its final impact analysis estimates eight confirmed user companies in 2021 and a modeled first-year cost range, not actual layoffs.

census.title: 2019 California retail pet-store sourcing ban

paragraphs.text: C-241  2019 California retail pet-store sourcing ban
Why this qualifies.  California pursued animal welfare by ending breeder-sourced pet sales in existing stores, materially restricting the stores and suppliers that depended on that trade.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  California | January 1, 2019. California required retail shops selling dogs, cats or rabbits to source them from shelters and rescue groups, ending ordinary breeder-sourced store sales to reduce puppy-mill harm.

Worksite and group record.  Pet stores that had relied on breeder-sourced animals and their suppliers lost that lawful retail channel; 2020 legislation later closed a remaining loophole. Store workers' overall job outcome requires store-level evidence.

Causation and legal limits.  Shelter/rescue placements, other pet products, direct breeder sales and a later amendment may offset or alter each business's material loss; do not assume every pet store was affected.
Further event evidence.  Match pre-2019 retail sales and supplier contracts to post-law activity and identify shops with a materially lost animal-sales line.

Sources and citation check.  AB 485, 2017 Statutes chapter 740 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov); Additional legal or source record (gov.ca.gov).  The chaptered 2017 statute and Governor's later summary establish the 2019 breeder-source restriction and 2020 tightening; impact by store remains to verify.

census.title: 2020 Maryland retail dog and cat sale ban

paragraphs.text: C-242  2020 Maryland retail dog and cat sale ban
Why this qualifies.  Maryland ended an established pet-store trade to protect animals, materially reducing the covered sales of existing shops and their supplier channel.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Maryland | January 1, 2020. Maryland prohibited retail pet stores from selling or otherwise transferring dogs and cats to address puppy- and kitten-mill harms, after a delayed implementation period.

Worksite and group record.  Existing pet shops selling cats and dogs lost their covered sales and supplying breeders lost a retail customer. The legislature's fiscal and policy note expressly anticipates lower taxable sales and a lost customer for small breeders.

Causation and legal limits.  Direct sales from breeders and shelter displays may continue; some stores did not sell covered animals and pet supplies remain. Actual firm and worker losses require transaction records.
Further event evidence.  Identify pre-ban retail pet licenses and sales, breeder contracts and post-ban animal sales or adoption arrangements.

Sources and citation check.  No More Puppy- and Kitten-Mills Act of 2018, chapter 237 (mgaleg.maryland.gov); Additional legal or source record (mgaleg.maryland.gov).  Enacted law gives the restriction and delayed date; legislative fiscal note describes lost retail sales and breeder channels without proving a specific store closure.

census.title: 2024 New York pet-store sale ban

paragraphs.text: C-243  2024 New York pet-store sale ban
Why this qualifies.  New York's animal-welfare law cut off a lawful animal-sales line for an existing, identifiable group of retail pet dealers.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.
Government action and scope.  New York State | December 15, 2024. New York barred pet stores from selling dogs, cats and rabbits statewide to stop the puppy-mill supply chain.

Worksite and group record.  Existing licensed pet dealers with retail stores lost the legal sale of those animals; the Attorney General sent a pre-effective-date notice to affected dealers and later described enforcement against a named pre-existing shop.

Causation and legal limits.  Animal adoptions and other pet products may continue; post-effective illegal sales are not compensable lawful work. Do not infer every licensed dealer or employee lost a primary income source.
Further event evidence.  Use pre-December 2024 license and sales records, later store status and lawful alternative revenue to measure the exposed group.

paragraphs.text: C-244  2019 New York City expanded-polystyrene foam ban
Why this qualifies.  New York City stopped an established foam-product market for environmental reasons, materially affecting specialized suppliers and some small users' costs.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  New York City | January 1, 2019; enforcement after June 30. New York City prohibited sale, use or possession of specified single-use expanded-polystyrene food containers and loose-fill packaging for waste-reduction purposes.

Worksite and group record.  The city's own notice identifies foam manufacturers, distributors, stores and food-service establishments as affected. Covered product makers and distributors lost that city market; small businesses faced replacement costs and could seek hardship waivers.

Causation and legal limits.  Prepackaged-food and raw-meat exceptions, warning period, substitutes and waivers narrow the affected group; later state foam law is a different action and overlapping losses must not be double-counted.
Further event evidence.  Find city foam suppliers and their pre-ban sales and workplaces, waiver decisions, substitute-product revenue and post-2022 statewide overlap.

census.title: Garrison Dam flooding of Fort Berthold land

paragraphs.text: C-245  Garrison Dam flooding of Fort Berthold land
Why this qualifies.  A federal dam built for broad flood-control and power benefits flooded established Fort Berthold homes and working land, materially burdening a concentrated community.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | 1946–1953 construction and filling. The United States built Garrison Dam for regional flood control, power and other public purposes, filling Lake Sakakawea on the Missouri River.

Worksite and group record.  GAO records 152,360 acres flooded on the Fort Berthold Reservation; Interior had estimated 289 families in the flood area. Homes, ranches and all of the reservation's irrigable land were affected.

Causation and legal limits.  Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
Further event evidence.  Reconcile the original land acquisition and tribal compensation records with affected farms, enterprises and later settlements.

Sources and citation check.  Pick–Sloan / Flood Control Act of 1944 (gao.gov); Additional legal or source record (nwo.usace.army.mil).  GAO Table 1 quantifies reservation flood acreage and family exposure; the Corps confirms project and public purposes.

census.title: Oahe Dam flooding of Cheyenne River and Standing Rock lands

paragraphs.text: C-246  Oahe Dam flooding of Cheyenne River and Standing Rock lands
Why this qualifies.  A federal public-benefit reservoir permanently flooded Cheyenne River and Standing Rock land, materially affecting established homes and land-based work.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | 1948–1960s construction and impoundment. The United States constructed Oahe Dam as part of the Missouri River system to reduce downstream flood risk and provide power, water and navigation benefits.

Worksite and group record.  GAO records 104,420 acres flooded on the Cheyenne River Reservation and 55,994 on Standing Rock, including valuable river bottoms, resources, structures and land-based livelihoods.

Causation and legal limits.  Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
Further event evidence.  Compare dam-specific land files, ranch and farm uses, relocation and compensation on the two reservations.

Sources and citation check.  Pick–Sloan / Flood Control Act of 1944 (gao.gov); Additional legal or source record (nwo.usace.army.mil).  GAO Table 1 ties both reservation areas to Oahe; the Corps describes system public purposes.

census.title: Fort Randall Dam flooding of reservation lands

paragraphs.text: C-247  Fort Randall Dam flooding of reservation lands
Why this qualifies.  Federal reservoir construction for regional benefits displaced families and working land on several reservations, with losses attributable to this dam to be separately measured.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | 1950s construction and filling. The United States built Fort Randall Dam for Missouri River flood control and related public power and water purposes.

Worksite and group record.  GAO ties this dam to lost land at Crow Creek, Lower Brule and Yankton; it reports 119 families displaced at Crow Creek and Lower Brule by Fort Randall, with 2,851 acres flooded at Yankton.

Causation and legal limits.  Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel. Crow Creek and Lower Brule total acreage in GAO combines this dam with Big Bend; do not assign all acreage twice.
Further event evidence.  Use dam-specific condemnation and relocation records to allocate losses separate from Big Bend and credit original and later compensation.

Sources and citation check.  Pick–Sloan / Flood Control Act of 1944 (gao.gov); Additional legal or source record (nwo.usace.army.mil).  GAO ties these reservations and 119 displaced families to Fort Randall; combined acreage cannot be split from its summary.

census.title: Big Bend Dam flooding of Crow Creek and Lower Brule lands

paragraphs.text: C-248  Big Bend Dam flooding of Crow Creek and Lower Brule lands
Why this qualifies.  Big Bend's federal public-benefit reservoir separately displaced an established Crow Creek and Lower Brule group, despite overlapping earlier flood effects.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | 1960s construction and filling. The United States constructed Big Bend Dam as another Missouri River flood-control and hydropower project.
Worksite and group record.  GAO reports 89 families displaced on Crow Creek and Lower Brule by Big Bend; the two reservations also lost land to Fort Randall.

Causation and legal limits.  Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel. Some families faced both projects, so the same loss cannot be counted twice.
Further event evidence.  Match parcel and household relocation across both dam projects, distinguishing incremental Big Bend harm and prior compensation.

census.title: Gavins Point Dam flooding of Santee land

paragraphs.text: C-249  Gavins Point Dam flooding of Santee land
Why this qualifies.  Federal dam construction for the wider Missouri basin permanently took a smaller group's established reservation land and resources.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | 1950s construction and filling. The United States built Gavins Point Dam within the Missouri River flood-control and power system.
Worksite and group record.  GAO identifies 593 acres of Santee Reservation land permanently flooded by this dam, with land and natural-resource impacts.

Causation and legal limits.  Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
Further event evidence.  Identify affected Santee parcels and uses, initial property payments and any subsequent compensation.

census.title: Grand Coulee Dam and Lake Roosevelt inundation

paragraphs.text: C-250  Grand Coulee Dam and Lake Roosevelt inundation
Why this qualifies.  A federal dam for national power and irrigation inundated established towns, homes and fishing places, materially affecting smaller resident and working groups.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Bureau of Reclamation and federal works agencies | 1933–1942 construction and filling. The federal government built Grand Coulee Dam and filled Lake Roosevelt to generate power, irrigate the Columbia Basin and support public works.

Worksite and group record.  The National Park Service reports that 11 river towns were lost and roughly 3,000 people left homes in the inundation zone; Kettle Falls and its longstanding salmon fishing place were also covered.

Causation and legal limits.  Residents, tribal fishing communities and town businesses had different land rights and redress histories. Do not treat everyone who moved as having the same unpaid livelihood loss.
Further event evidence.  Match flooded parcels, town enterprises and tribal fishing use to the original acquisition and later settlement records.

Sources and citation check.  Grand Coulee / Columbia Basin Project (home.nps.gov); Additional legal or source record (nps.gov).  NPS identifies the 11 lost towns, roughly 3,000 displaced people and the river-bottom communities; project purposes and compensation need individualized group review.

census.title: Norris Dam reservoir relocation in the Clinch Valley

paragraphs.text: C-251  Norris Dam reservoir relocation in the Clinch Valley
Why this qualifies.  TVA's public power and flood project displaced established Clinch Valley households and land-based work through the dam land program.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Tennessee Valley Authority | 1933–1936 construction. TVA built Norris Dam for flood control and power as its first planned hydroelectric project, acquiring and flooding upstream land.
Worksite and group record.  A National Park Service history says the project established a relocation protocol for families and grave sites; the Clinch Valley record describes community displacement.
Causation and legal limits.  The public source establishes an affected resident group but not a final family count or loss after land payments; some acquired owners could continue farms elsewhere.
Further event evidence.  Extract TVA purchase and relocation ledgers to identify farms, businesses and actual resettlement results.

census.title: Watauga Dam relocation of Butler, Tennessee

paragraphs.text: C-252  Watauga Dam relocation of Butler, Tennessee
Why this qualifies.  A federal flood-control and power project moved a preexisting agricultural town, materially affecting its households and place-bound livelihoods.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Tennessee Valley Authority | 1942–1948 construction and filling. TVA built Watauga Dam to control flooding and generate power and moved Butler, Tennessee, to higher ground before reservoir filling.
Worksite and group record.  TVA describes Butler as an agricultural town of about 650 families when work resumed; moving the whole town disrupted existing homes, farms and local businesses.
Causation and legal limits.  The 650 is a pre-project town-family figure, not a count of uncompensated moves or lost businesses; Butler was rebuilt and some activities resumed.
Further event evidence.  Use TVA relocation and property ledgers to distinguish land loss, resettlement, replacement enterprises and prior payment.

census.title: 1942 wartime exclusion and incarceration of Japanese Americans

paragraphs.text: C-253  1942 wartime exclusion and incarceration of Japanese Americans

Why this qualifies.  Federal exclusion orders asserted national defense while imposing devastating material loss on a smaller American group; later Congress rejected the premise and provided redress, which must be counted.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / War Department | 1942–1945. The federal government asserted a nationwide wartime-defense purpose, designated military areas and forcibly removed and incarcerated Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
Worksite and group record.  More than 120,000 people were uprooted; many lost homes, property, businesses and work. The displaced cohort included U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents.

Causation and legal limits.  Congress later recognized the action as a grave injustice rooted in racial prejudice and war hysteria, not a valid military necessity. The 1948 property-claims law and 1988 redress payments must be credited; this record does not suggest any additional individual entitlement.
Further event evidence.  Match business and work loss categories to contemporaneous records and the two redress programs, without relitigating the event's wrongful character.

Sources and citation check.  Executive Order 9066 and civilian exclusion orders (nps.gov); Additional legal or source record (archives.gov).  NPS documents the order and 120,000-plus forced removals; National Archives explains the later congressional apology and $20,000 redress. Stated national-security purpose is expressly described as a claim later repudiated.

paragraphs.text: C-254  1857 Seneca Village clearance for Central Park
Why this qualifies.  The city took and cleared an established smaller community for a public park, materially ending its homes, place-based cultivation and local institutions.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.
Government action and scope.  New York City | 1857. New York City used eminent domain to acquire Seneca Village land and remove residents to build a large public park for the growing city.

Causation and legal limits.  Original property payments, tenant status and subsequent work or housing need separate evidence; do not infer that all residents owned land or received no compensation.
Further event evidence.  Cross-check property award and census records against residents' homes, crops, businesses and tenancy.

Sources and citation check.  State-authorized eminent domain for Central Park (nyc.gov); Additional legal or source record (nycgovparks.org).  NYC Landmarks documents community displacement and resident count; NYC Parks supplies the public-park authorization and eminent-domain purpose.

paragraphs.text: C-255  1950s Southwest Washington urban renewal clearance

Government action and scope.  District of Columbia / federal redevelopment agencies | 1950s–1960s. Federal and District planners assembled and cleared Southwest Washington land for a public urban-renewal program intended to improve housing and the capital's economy.
Worksite and group record.  The National Capital Planning Commission reports 400 acres cleared, forced removal of 23,500 residents and displacement of local small businesses; many could not return.

Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  Michigan and United States / highway agencies | 1950s highway clearance. Michigan and federal highway agencies built I-375 to create an urban transportation link, with associated redevelopment in central Detroit.

Worksite and group record.  Federal Highway Administration records say the route and subsequent urban renewal largely demolished Paradise Valley and Black Bottom, established Black residential and business centers.

census.title: New London Fort Trumbull economic-development takings

paragraphs.text: C-257  New London Fort Trumbull economic-development takings
Why this qualifies.  A city used eminent domain on a smaller property group for a stated wider economic-development benefit, imposing a material land and place-based burden.

Causation and legal limits.  Original purchase or condemnation payments, temporary wartime jobs and later land use may offset different households differently; acreage is site size, not a count of uncompensated farms.

census.title: 1942 Los Alamos Manhattan Project land acquisition

paragraphs.text: C-259  1942 Los Alamos Manhattan Project land acquisition
Why this qualifies.  A federal wartime laboratory displaced an established small homesteading and school community to serve national defense.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | late 1942–1943. The Army acquired the Pajarito Plateau for the wartime weapons laboratory, removing homesteaders and closing the Los Alamos Ranch School.

Worksite and group record.  NPS records identify local Hispanic and other homesteaders who abandoned cabins and farm use; 12 homesteads remained with original owners and seven with their families at acquisition, while the established ranch school closed.

census.title: 1943 Hanford Manhattan Project land requisition

paragraphs.text: C-260  1943 Hanford Manhattan Project land requisition
Why this qualifies.  A national-defense land requisition removed established farms, homes and businesses in one local area for a wider wartime project.
Screening disposition.  Qualifying event for this register; worksite and group-specific effects remain to be measured.

Government action and scope.  United States / Army Corps of Engineers | March 1943 acquisition and removal. The United States took Columbia River land for the Hanford plutonium-production project, ordering residents out on short notice for wartime defense work.

Worksite and group record.  NPS reports roughly 1,500 residents in White Bluffs, Hanford, Richland and nearby communities affected, including farmers and local enterprises; some owners had 30–90 days to leave.
Causation and legal limits.  Initial settlements, wartime replacement work and Native land and use interests differ by group; the 1,500 is a population estimate, not a job-loss or unpaid-claim count.
Further event evidence.  Review requisition, farm and business records and original settlements; separate tribal use interests from private holdings.

Sources and citation check.  Manhattan Project Hanford site land requisition (nps.gov); Additional legal or source record (nps.gov).  NPS identifies communities, approximate resident group and short notice; site-specific compensation must be reconciled.
